title: A Sequential Multiple Assignment Randomized Trial Design with Response-Adaptive Tailoring Function
abstract: We present a novel sequential multiple assignment randomized trial (SMART) design that integrates response-adaptive randomization with tailoring functions (RA-TF-SMART). We develop percentile-based and Z-score RA-TFs that incorporate both within-patient and between-patient adaptation to map continuous outcomes to randomization probabilities. We apply Q-learning, tree-based reinforcement learning, and G-estimation to estimate dynamic treatment regimens (DTRs). We compare our RA-TF-SMART designs to balanced randomized SMARTs (BR-SMARTs), tailoring function SMARTs (TF-SMARTs), and generalized outcome-adaptive SMARTs (GO-SMARTs). This study addresses limitations in SMART methodology by presenting designs where randomization probability does not require dichotomization of continuous outcomes and utilizes both individual patient outcomes and accumulated treatment efficacy data from prior participants. output.evidence_of_randomization: The abstract describes a "sequential multiple assignment randomized trial (SMART) design that integrates response-adaptive randomization" and mentions "randomization probability" and "randomized SMARTs," but does not specify how individual participants were allocated to treatment groups. The focus is on methodological design and simulation rather than empirical patient allocation.
output.reasoning: This manuscript analyzes data, but the data are entirely simulated rather than from actual patients. The abstract describes a novel SMART methodology with response-adaptive randomization and presents comparisons of different design approaches using simulation. While the paper discusses randomization concepts and trial design, it does not report results from an actual randomized controlled trial evaluating patient-level health outcomes. Instead, it is a methodological paper developing and comparing statistical/design frameworks. The outcomes being evaluated appear to be statistical properties of the designs (e.g., DTR estimation validity) rather than patient health outcomes. This does not meet the criteria for CONSORT compliance review, which targets empirical trials with real patient data and health outcomes.
